why:
Two independent decisions have to be made: the mode of vibration, and whether the wave travels.

**Mode.** In a sound wave in air the particles of the medium vibrate back and forth *along* the direction in which the disturbance advances, producing alternate compressions (crowded, high-pressure regions) and rarefactions (widely separated, low-pressure regions). That is the definition of a longitudinal wave, and the chapter states it directly: sound waves are longitudinal waves.

**Travelling or stationary.** The sound leaves the sitar and reaches the listener, carrying energy outward from the source to a distant point. A wave that does this is a progressive (travelling) wave. A stationary wave is instead the superposition of two identical waves travelling in opposite directions; it transports no net energy along its length, so it cannot be what carries the music across the room.

The two transverse choices fail on physics, not on wording: a transverse mechanical wave needs the medium to possess **elasticity of shape**, and a gas has none — air cannot sustain the shear a transverse disturbance requires. That is why transverse mechanical waves travel through solids and along liquid surfaces only. The stationary choices fail because nothing here sets up two oppositely-directed waves.

So the wave is **longitudinal** and **progressive**.

The quantity fixed at the boundary is the one set by the **source**, not by the medium.

The sitar string, tuning fork or loudspeaker producing the sound vibrates a definite number of times per second, and every one of those vibrations must be passed on across the air-water boundary — wavefronts cannot pile up at the surface or be destroyed there. So the number of wavefronts arriving in the water each second equals the number leaving the air each second: the **frequency is unchanged**.

The speed, by contrast, is a property of the medium, fixed by its elastic modulus and density: about 340 m/s in air against about 1500 m/s in water. So the speed certainly changes.

And since \(\mathrm{v} = n\lambda\) with \(n\) held fixed, the wavelength must change in exactly the same ratio as the speed — roughly four-and-a-half times longer in water. The chapter puts it in one line: when a sound wave goes from one medium to another its velocity changes along with its wavelength, while its frequency, which is decided by the source, remains constant.

Because two of the three quantities do change, the "all of above" alternative is false as well. Only the **frequency** stays the same.

The question is what Newton got *wrong*, since the correction exists to repair it.

Newton assumed the compressions and rarefactions of a sound wave happen slowly enough for heat to leak away and keep the temperature of the air constant. On that assumption the relevant elastic constant is the **isothermal** bulk modulus, which for a gas obeying Boyle's law is just the pressure \(P\), giving \(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{P/\rho}\). Putting in NTP values this yields about 280 m/s, while the measured speed is 332 m/s — roughly 16% too low, far more than experimental error could explain.

Laplace identified the flaw. At an audible frequency of, say, 256 Hz the air at any point is compressed and rarefied 256 times every second. That is far too fast for the heat generated on compression to be conducted away before the rarefaction arrives, so no heat enters or leaves the element: the process is **adiabatic**. The adiabatic modulus is \(\gamma P\), and \(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{\gamma P/\rho}\) with \(\gamma = 1.41\) gives 332.3 m/s, in close agreement with experiment.

The isothermal alternative is precisely Newton's mistaken premise — the thing the correction removes, not the reason for it. That sound waves are longitudinal is true, but Newton's formula already describes a longitudinal wave, so it explains no discrepancy. Wavelength enters the derivation nowhere at all.

The correction is needed because the propagation is **adiabatic**.

The speed of a mechanical wave is set by the elastic and inertial properties of the medium, \(\mathrm{v} = \sqrt{E/\rho}\). Going from a gas to a liquid to a solid, the elastic modulus \(E\) rises by many orders of magnitude while the density \(\rho\) rises only by about three, so the ratio — and hence the speed — increases steeply. Solids are also the only media with elasticity of shape as well as of volume, and their atoms are the most strongly and closely coupled, so a disturbance is handed on fastest there.

The chapter's own Table 8.1 settles it numerically: air at 20 \(^\circ\)C 343 m/s and helium 965 m/s; water at 20 \(^\circ\)C 1482 m/s and seawater 1522 m/s; then copper 3560, steel 5941, granite 6000 and aluminium 6420 m/s. Every solid listed beats every liquid, and every liquid beats every gas.

A vacuum is not merely the slowest case — it is not a case at all. Sound is a mechanical wave and needs a material medium to carry it, so it does not propagate through a vacuum and no speed can be quoted.

The speed is therefore greatest in a **solid**.

In a closed hall the same note reaches a listener many times over: once directly, and again after bouncing off the walls, roof and floor. If those repeated reflections persist, one note is still being heard when the next is played and the music is smeared into a continuous blur of increased loudness that cannot be heard clearly — this is **reverberation**. If a reflecting surface is far enough away (more than about 15 m, so the delay exceeds the 0.1 s our hearing retains a sound for) the repetition is heard as a distinct **echo** instead. Both spoil music, so both must be suppressed.

The chapter prescribes exactly one remedy for the walls: reverberation is decreased by making walls and roofs rough and by hanging curtains to avoid reflection, with chairs and wall surfaces covered in sound-absorbing materials such as porous cardboard sheets, perforated acoustic tiles and gypsum boards; and echoes are reduced by making the reflecting surfaces more absorptive. Absorbing walls remove the reflected energy at source.

Walls that **reflected** sound would do the opposite, feeding reverberation and echo. (The chapter does want the single surface *directly behind the performer* to be reflecting and parabolic, so that sound is spread evenly outward from its focus — but that is one shaped surface serving loudness, not the walls of the hall.) Walls that **transmitted** sound would let the music leak out and street noise leak in, whereas a good auditorium must be sound-proof when closed. **Amplifying** is the job of the sound system; a passive wall supplies no energy and cannot amplify anything.

The walls should therefore **absorb sound**.
